metadata.title: Effects of individual attributes, family background, and school context on students’ global competence: Insights from the OECD PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata for global competence and applies the complex sampling design through hierarchical linear modelling (HLM). The authors state that both student-level weights (to adjust for non-participating students) and school-level weights (to adjust for oversampling of schools with underrepresented minority students) were considered in the model. This indicates that estimates are intended to be representative of the target populations within each participating country/region, while accounting for the two-level sampling structure (students nested within schools and countries). The paper does not report replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it does not describe additional preprocessing such as outlier trimming or grade filtering beyond the PISA global competence domain and the selected six countries/regions.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample is restricted to six PISA 2018 countries/regions (Chile, Panama, Croatia, Malta, Korea, Hong Kong) because these are the only ones that administered the global competence cognitive test and also had the full set of student, parent, and school questionnaires needed for the study’s individual, family, and school context variables. The dependent variable is PISA 2018 global competence performance, for which 10 plausible values are computed per student; the authors use weighted likelihood estimates (WLE) as participant scores. Missing data in PISA are described as missing at random due to random assignment of testlets, and the authors apply multiple imputation to impute missing data rather than listwise deletion. No additional exclusions (e.g., outlier removal) are reported in the provided text.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Global competence (15-year-olds; OECD global citizenship framework)
main_findings.target_variable: Global competence performance (WLE from 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: HLM regression coefficients (β) reported by country; e.g., Gender: Chile β=-9.81***, Korea β=-15.25***, Hong Kong β=-10.02***, Croatia β=-9.91***, Panama β=-7.26***, Malta β=-21.97***. Global self-efficacy: Chile β=11.86***, Korea β=19.14***, Hong Kong β=17.86***, Croatia β=14.23***, Panama β=10.62***, Malta β=22.90***. ESCS: Chile β=8.95***, Korea β=11.83***, Hong Kong β=4.11***, Croatia β=9.34***, Panama β=4.98***, Malta β=17.37***. Teachers’ intercultural attitudes: Chile β=32.91***, Korea β=23.61***, Hong Kong β=29.50***, Croatia β=18.14***, Panama β=19.97***, Malta β=30.77***.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Global competence (15-year-olds; OECD global citizenship framework) the study leveraged Gender, Global self-efficacy, Family ESCS, and Teachers’ intercultural attitudes to predict Global competence performance (WLE from 10 plausible values), finding that these factors significantly relate to students’ global competence across all six countries/regions, with female students scoring higher than male students and higher self-efficacy, ESCS, and teacher intercultural attitudes associated with higher global competence. This indicates that strengthening teacher intercultural training and supporting students’ global self-efficacy—while addressing socioeconomic disparities—may improve global competence outcomes, though the correlational HLM design does not establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 global competence for 15-year-olds using a hierarchical linear modelling approach to examine how individual attributes, family background, and school context relate to global competence across six countries/regions (Chile, Panama, Croatia, Malta, Korea, Hong Kong). Global competence is measured via a cognitive test and scaled using 10 plausible values, with weighted likelihood estimates (WLE) used as participant scores; the paper reports country-specific HLM coefficients rather than ML predictive accuracy. Across all six regions, gender, student self-efficacy in global issues, family ESCS, and teachers’ intercultural attitudes show statistically significant associations with global competence (e.g., gender β ranges from −7.26 to −21.97; self-efficacy β ranges from 10.62 to 22.90; ESCS β ranges from 4.11 to 17.37; teacher attitudes β ranges from 18.14 to 32.91). The authors apply student- and school-level sampling weights and use multiple imputation for missing data, but the design is explicitly correlational, so causal claims are limited.
